usage: Refers specifically to the big lunar holidays 설날 and 추석, not just any day off.
The standard greeting you say to coworkers and neighbors before the break; pairs with 보내다, never 지내다 here.
명절 plus 연휴; the multi-day stretch most people get off work.
증후군 = syndrome; the real exhaustion (especially for women cooking) that the news discusses every year.
examples: 이번 명절에 고향에 내려가요?
Are you going to your hometown this holiday?
내려가다 = to go down (to one's hometown); a classic holiday small-talk opener.
명절만 되면 고속도로가 꽉 막혀요.
Whenever a holiday comes around the highways are completely jammed.
-만 되면 = every single time it becomes; the famous 명절 gridlock.
저는 명절에 일하는 대신 평일에 쉬어요.
Instead of working on the holiday I take weekdays off.
-는 대신(에) = in exchange for / instead of; common for service-industry workers.
nuance: 명절 (漢字 名節, 'name-occasion / notable festival') is the word reserved for Korea's two great lunar-calendar reunions, 설날 (Lunar New Year) and 추석 (the harvest festival), when the whole country travels home to family — so it carries a heavy weight of family duty, ancestral rites, and obligatory cooking that a neutral day off never has. The sharp contrast to learn is 명절 vs 공휴일 (公休日, 'public-rest-day'): every 명절 is a 공휴일, but most 공휴일 (광복절, 현충일, a single Monday off) are NOT 명절. It also differs from 기념일 (記念日), an 'anniversary / commemorative day' like a wedding anniversary. Register is everyday-polite; asking 명절 잘 보내셨어요? is warm, slightly personal small talk. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 명절 like the generic word 'holiday' and stretching it over Christmas or a random vacation day — and saying 명절 축하해요, since Koreans bless the holiday with 잘 보내세요, not 'congratulations.'

mistakes: Don't use 명절 for every public holiday: a single day off like 광복절 or 어린이날 is a 공휴일, while 명절 means specifically the big lunar reunions 설날 and 추석.
Saying 명절 축하해요 sounds off because 축하 ('congratulations') is for achievements; for a holiday you wish 명절 잘 보내세요 (spend the holiday well).
English 'holiday' = any vacation, but 명절 ≠ 휴가 (personal leave) or 방학 (school break); a beach trip in July is 휴가, not 명절.

usage: A softer, purely-Korean name for 추석; favored in greetings and on cards.
The set holiday greeting you'll get by text from companies and friends.
may it always be as good as Chuseok
From the proverb 더도 말고 덜도 말고 한가위만 같아라 ('no more, no less, just like Chuseok').
풍성하다 = plentiful/bountiful; a fixed warm collocation for the harvest holiday.
examples: 행복한 한가위 보내세요!
Have a happy Chuseok!
The most common holiday-greeting text you'll send and receive.
한가위에는 보름달을 보면서 소원을 빌어요.
On Chuseok people make a wish while looking at the full moon.
보름달 = full moon; 소원을 빌다 = to make a wish, the fixed verb pairing.
한가위는 추석을 부르는 정겨운 우리말이에요.
Hangawi is the heart-warming native-Korean name for Chuseok.
정겹다 = warm/fond; explains the relationship between the two words.
nuance: 한가위 is the warm, indigenous (순우리말, NOT Sino-Korean) name for 추석 (秋夕, 'autumn-evening'), the harvest festival on the 15th of the eighth lunar month. The pieces are 한 ('big / great,' as in 한길, 한복판) plus 가위, an old word tied to 가운데 ('middle') — so it evokes 'the great middle (full-moon) day' of autumn. The key contrast is purely one of register, not meaning: 한가위 and 추석 are the same day, but 한가위 sounds friendlier and more lyrical, so 행복한 한가위 보내세요 feels gentler than the plain 추석 잘 보내세요. You'll meet it most in greetings, cards, and the proverb 더도 말고 덜도 말고 한가위만 같아라, a wish that life were always this bountiful. The English-speaker pitfall is assuming it is a separate holiday from 추석 (it is the very same one) and mis-spelling the final syllable as 의 — it is 위, the same shape as 위 'above.'

It's spelled 한가위 (ending in 위), not 한가의 — the last syllable is the vowel 위, not 의.
Because 한가위 is native Korean, don't try to write it in 한자; only 추석 (秋夕) has a hanja form.

usage: Several days off in a row; the thing everyone plans trips around.
황금 = golden; an extra-long break when holidays line up with the weekend.
계획 = plan; a standard topic of conversation before the break.
징검다리 = stepping stones; when a workday sits between two days off, often taken as leave to bridge them.
examples: 이번 추석은 연휴가 길어서 좋아요.
This Chuseok the long weekend is nice and long.
-아서 좋다 = good because; people love when 연휴 stretches out.
연휴라 비행기표가 다 매진됐어요.
Because it's a long weekend the plane tickets are all sold out.
-(이)라(서) = because it is; 매진되다 = to sell out, demand spikes during 연휴.
연휴 잘 보내고 오세요.
Enjoy the long weekend (and come back well).
A natural send-off to coworkers before the break; -고 오다 = do it and come back.
nuance: 연휴 (漢字 連休, literally 連 'connect / link' + 休 'rest' — 'linked-up rest days') means a run of consecutive days off, the practical block of time Koreans actually organize trips around rather than a single ceremonial holiday. The crucial trio to keep apart: 연휴 = multiple days off in a row on everyone's calendar; 휴일 (休日) = a single day off; and 휴가 (休暇) = your personal, individually-taken vacation leave. So 'I'm taking 연휴 next week' is wrong if you simply mean private time off — that's 휴가. When a 명절 or public holiday connects to a weekend it becomes a 황금연휴 (golden long weekend), and people often burn a vacation day on a 징검다리 (stepping-stone) workday to bridge the gap. Flights and KTX seats sell out fast, so locals book early. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 연휴 onto 'a holiday' (singular event) — 연휴 is fundamentally about the unbroken stretch of days, not the holiday's meaning.

usage: The morning ceremony honoring ancestors held on 설날 and 추석.
지내다 is the fixed verb for holding the ceremony, never 하다.
상 = table/spread; the array of food set out for the 차례.
The dishes (전, 나물, 송편/떡국, fruit) prepared specifically for the ceremony.
examples: 설날 아침에 차례를 지내고 떡국을 먹어요.
On Seollal morning we hold the ancestral rite and then eat tteokguk.
The standard sequence of a Lunar New Year morning; -고 links the two steps.
요즘은 차례를 간소하게 지내는 집도 많아요.
These days many households hold the rite in a simplified way.
간소하게 = simply/plainly; reflects a real modern trend.
저희 집은 차례를 안 지내고 여행을 가요.
Our family doesn't do the rite and travels instead.
저희 = humble 'our'; increasingly common among younger families.
nuance: 차례 (漢字 茶禮, literally 茶 'tea' + 禮 'rite' — historically a simple 'tea offering') is the streamlined ancestral memorial held on the morning of the two 명절, 설날 and 추석, where the family sets out a 차례상 of food and bows to honor all the ancestors together. The single most important contrast is 차례 vs 제사 (祭祀): 제사 is the solemn rite held at night on the death-anniversary (기일) of one specific ancestor, while 차례 is the lighter, daytime, holiday rite for the ancestors collectively — so they are not interchangeable. The locked-in verb is 지내다 (차례를 지내다 / 제사를 지내다); 차례를 하다 sounds wrong to natives. Register is neutral-descriptive, but the topic is culturally weighty. Increasingly, younger households 차례를 간소하게 지내다 (simplify it) or skip it to travel, which is now broadly accepted. The English-speaker pitfall: do not gloss 차례 as a generic 'ceremony' or pair it with 하다 — and do not confuse this homograph with the other 차례 meaning 'turn / sequence' (as in 차례차례, '목차/table of contents'), which is a different word entirely.

Don't confuse this 차례 (ancestral rite) with the everyday homograph 차례 meaning 'turn/order' (네 차례야 = 'it's your turn'); same spelling, unrelated meaning.

english: New Year's deep bow to elders
usage: The formal full bow children and juniors make on 설날.
to make the New Year's bow
하다 verb; what you do toward grandparents and parents on Seollal.
Cash elders give after receiving a 세배; note the 사이시옷 and read it '세배똔'.
Happy New Year (lit. receive many blessings)
The set line you say while performing the 세배.
examples: 설날에 할머니께 세배를 했어요.
On Seollal I made the deep bow to my grandmother.
께 is the honorific 'to' (raising 할머니); bowing to elders is the core ritual.
세배하면 어른들이 세뱃돈을 주세요.
When you do the New Year's bow, the elders give you money.
-(으)면 = when/if; the cause-and-effect kids look forward to most.
세배할 때 '새해 복 많이 받으세요'라고 말해요.
While bowing you say 'Happy New Year.'
-라고 말하다 = to say (direct quote); the standard accompanying line.
nuance: 세배 (漢字 歲拜, literally 歲 'year / age' + 拜 'to bow' — 'the year-bow') is the deep, formal 큰절 that younger people offer to elders on the morning of 설날 to wish them well for the year, performed together with 새해 복 많이 받으세요. The contrast to fix in mind is 세배 vs the everyday 인사 (人事, 'greeting') and the plain verb 절(을) 하다 ('to bow'): a 세배 is one specific kneeling New-Year bow, not any nod or hello, and it is distinct from a 묵념 (silent tribute) or a funeral bow. The fixed verb is 세배(를) 하다; you make it 'to' an elder with the honorific particle 께, and the elder receives it (세배를 받다). In return they give 덕담 (words of blessing) and 세뱃돈 (New Year's cash). The English-speaker pitfalls: (1) don't confuse 세배 (the bow) with 세뱃돈 (the money that follows) — related but different words; (2) note the 사이시옷 in 세뱃돈, pronounced '세배똔'; and (3) since 세배 already contains 절 (a bow), saying 세배를 절하다 is redundant.

세배 is the proper kneeling 큰절 to elders, not a casual nod; performing it carelessly reads as disrespectful.
Use the honorific 께 ('to an elder'), not 에게/한테: 할머니께 세배를 했어요, because you are raising the recipient's status.

usage: Kind, encouraging wishes elders give, especially at New Year.
하다 verb; what an elder does after receiving your 세배.
나누다 = to share; people trade 덕담 around the holiday table.
한마디 = a word/remark; 'say a few kind words' on a happy occasion.
examples: 세배를 하면 어른들이 덕담을 해 주세요.
After you bow, the elders offer words of blessing.
해 주다 = do (for someone); the elder's half of the 세배 exchange.
새해에는 건강하라는 덕담을 많이 들었어요.
For the new year I heard lots of wishes to stay healthy.
건강하라는 = the quoted wish 'be healthy'; typical New Year 덕담.
결혼식에서 어른이 덕담 한마디 해 주셨어요.
At the wedding an elder said a few words of blessing.
해 주시다 (honorific); 덕담 isn't only for New Year — it fits any happy occasion.
nuance: 덕담 (漢字 德談, literally 德 'virtue / goodness' + 談 'talk' — 'virtuous, goodness-bringing speech') means the warm, forward-looking words of blessing an elder gives to younger people, most famously right after receiving a 세배 on 설날 (건강해라, 시험 잘 봐라, 좋은 사람 만나라). The contrast to internalize is 덕담 vs 충고 (忠告, 'frank advice') and 잔소리 ('nagging'): 덕담 is purely positive, well-wishing, and uplifting, whereas 충고 points out what to fix and 잔소리 scolds — so an elder telling you to study harder in a critical tone is NOT giving 덕담. It also differs from 칭찬 (praise for something already done), since 덕담 wishes good things for the future. The fixed verbs are 덕담을 하다 / 나누다 / 건네다; 덕담을 말하다 sounds unnatural. Register: spoken by a senior to a junior, or exchanged among peers at celebrations. The English-speaker pitfall is using 덕담 for any 'good word' including constructive criticism — if it stings or corrects, it isn't 덕담 — and pairing it with 말하다 instead of 하다/나누다.

english: rice-cake soup eaten on New Year
usage: Thinly sliced rice cakes in clear broth; the must-eat dish on 설날 morning.
Eating a bowl on New Year symbolically adds a year to your age.
그릇 = bowl (the counter); also the joking 'unit' of aging one year.
A popular variant with 만두 (dumplings) added to the same broth.
examples: 설날 아침에는 떡국을 꼭 먹어요.
On Seollal morning we always eat tteokguk.
꼭 = without fail; the defining New Year food custom.
떡국 한 그릇 먹으면 한 살 더 먹는 거예요.
Eating a bowl of tteokguk means you turn a year older.
한 살 더 먹다 = to gain a year; -는 거예요 explains the custom.
저는 떡국보다 떡만둣국을 더 좋아해요.
I like rice-cake-and-dumpling soup more than plain tteokguk.
-보다 더 = more than; comparing the two versions.
nuance: 떡국 is a 합성어 (compound) of pure-Korean 떡 ('rice cake') + 국 ('soup'), so it literally means 'rice-cake soup' — thin oval slices of 가래떡 simmered in a clear beef or anchovy broth, eaten on the morning of 설날. The long-running joke 떡국 한 그릇 = 한 살 ('one bowl, one year older') ties it to the lunar tradition where everyone aged together at New Year, so people still tease 떡국 몇 그릇 먹었어? to ask, half-jokingly, how old you are. Contrast it with two other 떡 dishes: 떡볶이 (spicy stir-fried rice-cake snack — savory-sweet, a totally different cylinder of 떡) and 떡만둣국 (the heartier 떡국 + 만두 variant). The verb is simply 떡국을 먹다 / 끓이다. The English-speaker pitfall: don't conflate 떡국 with 떡볶이 just because both contain 떡, and remember the 'aging' line is folklore — since Korea's 2023 switch to international 만 나이, eating 떡국 has no bearing on your legal age.

Don't conflate 떡국 with 떡볶이 just because both contain 떡, and remember the 'aging' line is folklore — since Korea's 2023 switch to international 만 나이, eating 떡국 has no bearing on your legal age.

The rice cake in 떡국 (sliced 가래떡) isn't the same as the chewy cylinders in 떡볶이; 떡 is a broad category, so naming the dish, not just '떡,' avoids confusion.

usage: Stuffed, pine-steamed rice cakes; the signature 추석 food.
빚다 is the special verb for forming dough (and pottery) by hand.
깨 = sesame; a common filling, alongside 콩 (beans), 밤 (chestnut), 팥 (red bean).
솔잎 = pine needles; 송편 is steamed over them, which gives it its scent.
examples: 추석에는 온 가족이 모여서 송편을 빚어요.
On Chuseok the whole family gathers to make songpyeon.
온 가족 = the whole family; making them together is the tradition.
송편을 예쁘게 빚으면 예쁜 딸을 낳는대요.
They say if you shape songpyeon prettily you'll have a pretty daughter.
-(ㄴ/는)대요 = they say (reported); a well-known playful old saying.
저는 깨송편이 제일 맛있어요.
Sesame songpyeon is the tastiest to me.
제일 = most/best; naming a favorite filling.
nuance: 송편 (the 송 is 漢字 松 'pine,' + native 편/떡 for the cake, so roughly 'pine(-steamed) rice cake') are small half-moon-shaped 떡 stuffed with sesame, beans, or chestnut and steamed over a layer of 솔잎 (pine needles), eaten at 추석 / 한가위. The verb to lock in is 빚다 — the special hand-forming verb also used for shaping pottery and brewing rice wine — so traditionally you say 송편을 빚다, not the plain 송편을 만들다 (which natives understand but find flatter). Contrast 송편 with the New-Year rice cake in 떡국 (sliced 가래떡, savory, in soup) and with generic 떡: 송편 is one specific shaped, filled, sweet-ish, pine-steamed variety tied to autumn, the half-moon shape echoing the harvest moon. A charming saying claims neatly-made 송편 foretells a pretty daughter. The English-speaker pitfall is defaulting to 만들다 for the verb and treating 송편 as interchangeable with any 떡 — it is the 추석 cake specifically, just as 떡국's slices belong to 설날.

usage: Visiting ancestors' graves to pay respects, especially at 추석 and 설날.
가다 verb; the family outing to the gravesite during the holiday.
벌초 = cutting the overgrown grass on the mound, usually done before 추석.
산소 = the burial mound you visit; the respectful word for a grave.
examples: 추석에 가족들이랑 성묘를 다녀왔어요.
I went to visit the family graves with relatives for Chuseok.
다녀오다 = go and come back; 이랑 = casual 'with' (spoken).
성묘 가기 전에 벌초부터 했어요.
Before the grave visit we did the grass-cutting first.
-기 전에 = before doing; -부터 = starting with, 벌초 precedes 성묘.
요즘은 성묘 대신 납골당에 가는 사람도 많아요.
These days many people go to a columbarium instead of tending graves.
납골당 = charnel house/columbarium; reflects changing burial customs.
nuance: 성묘 (漢字 省墓, literally 省 'to look in on / examine' + 墓 'grave' — 'to look in on the grave') is the custom of visiting ancestors' burial mounds to tidy them and bow in respect, done above all at 추석 and 설날. Distinguish three linked terms: 성묘 is the whole respectful visit; 벌초 (伐草, 'cut the grass') is the specific chore of clearing weeds off the 산소 (山所), usually done a week or two before the holiday; and 차례 is the food-table rite performed back at home — so 성묘 (at the grave) and 차례 (at home) are different parts of the holiday, not synonyms. The verb is 성묘(를) 가다 / 다녀오다. Note 산소 vs 무덤: 무덤 is the plain word 'grave,' while 산소 is the polite, respectful term used for one's own ancestors. As cremation has become the norm, families increasingly visit a 납골당 (columbarium) instead, yet 성묘 still covers paying these respects. The English-speaker pitfall is collapsing 성묘 / 벌초 / 차례 into one 'grave ceremony' — they are distinct steps — and using 무덤 where the respectful 산소 is expected for your own family.

english: the 15th of the lunar month; full-moon day
usage: The midpoint of a lunar month, when the moon is full.
the first full moon of the year
정월 = first lunar month; a traditional holiday on its 15th.
달 = moon; the round moon seen on a 보름 night.
동안 = during; 보름 also colloquially means a span of roughly 15 days.
examples: 정월대보름에는 부럼을 깨 먹어요.
On the first full moon we crack and eat nuts (burum).
부럼 = nuts cracked for health; 깨 먹다 = crack and eat, a 대보름 custom.
오늘 밤 보름달이 정말 크고 밝아요.
Tonight's full moon is really big and bright.
보름달 = full moon; a natural everyday remark.
여행 간 지 벌써 보름이 지났어요.
It's already been about half a month since the trip.
-(ㄴ) 지 ... 지나다 = it's been (time) since; 보름 here = ~15 days.
nuance: 보름 is a pure-Korean word (NOT Sino-Korean) marking the 15th day of the lunar month — the night of the full moon — and by natural extension a casual span of 'about half a month.' Contrast the components in the holiday name 정월대보름 (正月大보름): 정월 (正月) = the first lunar month, 대 (大) = 'great,' so it's 'the great full moon of the first month,' when people crack 부럼 nuts and eat 오곡밥 (five-grain rice) and 나물 for health and luck. Keep three things separate: 보름 (the 15th / full-moon day or a ~15-day span), 보름달 (the full moon you see in the sky), and 정월대보름 (the actual holiday) — so don't shorten the holiday to just '보름.' Also distinguish the duration sense: 보름 ≈ 15 days, whereas 'two weeks' is 2주(일) = 14 days, so they aren't identical. In everyday speech you'll hear it most as 보름달. The English-speaker pitfall is reading 보름 as exactly 14 days like 'a fortnight,' and treating 보름달 (the moon) as if it were the holiday.

english: the dog days of summer (hottest days)
usage: The three hottest marked days of summer: 초복, 중복, 말복.
삼복 = the three bok days; 더위 = heat — the fiercest stretch of summer.
eat samgyetang on a bok day
The custom of eating hot ginseng-chicken soup to fight heat with heat.
The three 복날 spread across mid-to-late summer, about ten days apart.
examples: 복날이라 삼계탕집 앞에 줄이 길어요.
It's a bok day so the line in front of the samgyetang place is long.
-(이)라 = because it's; eating 삼계탕 on 복날 causes famous lunchtime queues.
오늘이 초복인데 보양식 먹으러 갈까요?
Today's the first bok day — shall we go eat some restorative food?
보양식 = stamina food; -(으)러 가다 = go in order to, -ㄹ까요 invites.
삼복더위에는 밖에 나가기도 싫어요.
During the peak-bok heat I don't even want to go outside.
-기도 싫다 = don't even want to; conveys the brutal heat.
nuance: 복날 is a hybrid word: the 복 is 漢字 伏 ('to lie low / crouch,' the same 伏 in 복병 'ambush'), evoking heat so heavy that even the autumn 'metal' energy lies prostrate before it, plus native 날 ('day') — so '복날' is 'the crouching-heat day.' There are three each summer — 초복 (初伏, first), 중복 (中伏, mid), 말복 (末伏, last) — set ~10 days apart and collectively called 삼복 (三伏), the time of 삼복더위 (peak heat). The custom is 이열치열 (以熱治熱, 'fight heat with heat'): eat a steaming 보양식 (補養食, restorative dish) like 삼계탕 or 추어탕, which is why famous soup shops get long lunchtime lines. Two cautions: 복날 is NOT a single fixed date but three separate days, so name 초복/중복/말복 when you mean one; and this 복 (伏 'crouch') is unrelated to the 복 (福 'fortune') in 새해 복 — same sound, different hanja. The English-speaker pitfall is assuming peak-heat days call for cold food: the 복날 tradition is deliberately hot soup, so 'I'll eat 냉면 to celebrate 복날' misses the 이열치열 logic.

Despite the heat, the 복날 custom is piping-hot soup (이열치열), not cold food — saying you'll eat 냉면 to 'celebrate' 복날 misses the point.
The 복 in 복날 is 伏 ('crouch/lie low'), not the 福 ('fortune/luck') in 복 많이 받으세요; don't read 복날 as a 'lucky day.'

usage: Worn on 명절, at weddings and first-birthdays, and now for photos at palaces.
입다 = to wear (clothes on the body); the verb for putting on the outfit.
대여 = rental; you rent 한복 to enter Seoul's palaces free.
생활 = daily living; a modernized, casual version made for daily wear.
examples: 설날에 한복을 입고 세배를 했어요.
On Seollal I wore hanbok and did the New Year's bow.
-고 = and (sequence); wearing 한복 for the 명절 rite is the classic occasion.
경복궁은 한복을 입으면 입장료가 무료예요.
Gyeongbokgung is free admission if you wear hanbok.
-(으)면 = if; 무료 = free, a popular reason young people rent 한복.
요즘은 생활한복을 평소에 입는 사람도 있어요.
These days some people wear modern hanbok in everyday life.
평소에 = normally/usually; reflects the 생활한복 trend.
nuance: 한복 (漢字 韓服, literally 韓 'Korea / Korean' + 服 'clothing' — 'Korean dress'; the 服 is the same character in 교복 'school uniform,' 양복 'Western suit') is traditional Korean clothing — for women the 저고리 (jacket) and 치마 (skirt), for men 저고리 and 바지 — worn most on 명절, at weddings, and at 돌 (first-birthday) parties. The verb is firmly 입다, the body-clothing 'wear' verb, which contrasts with Korean's other 'wear' verbs: 쓰다 (hats, glasses — 모자를 쓰다), 신다 (shoes, socks — 신발을 신다), and 차다 (a watch — 시계를 차다). So 한복을 쓰다 or 한복을 신다 is wrong. Compare 한복 (Korean) with 양복 (洋服, a Western men's suit) and 교복 (校服, school uniform) — all share 服. For young people and tourists, 한복 대여 near palaces like 경복궁 is popular because wearing it gives free admission and great photos, and a modernized 생활한복 is rising as casual daily wear. The English-speaker pitfall is borrowing English 'wear' (one verb for everything) and reaching for 쓰다/신다, plus dismissing 한복 as a museum costume when rental and 생활한복 culture is thriving among 20–30s.
